content.title: About
content.content: Sorghum flour is made from whole sorghum grains (Sorghum bicolor). It is a gluten‑free flour with a mild nutty aroma and soft texture, commonly used in baking, breading, and as a thickener for sauces.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Sorghum is one of the oldest cultivated cereals, grown for over 5,000 years.
Sorghum flour contains no gluten, making it suitable for gluten‑free diets.
The crop is drought‑tolerant and can thrive in regions with limited water resources.
It is often blended with other gluten‑free flours to improve baked‑good structure.
Sorghum is rich in antioxidants, including phenolic compounds.

items.title: High in fiber
items.content: Fiber supports healthy digestion and promotes a feeling of fullness.

items.title: Source of iron
items.content: Iron is essential for oxygen transport in the blood and energy production.

items.title: Contains magnesium
items.content: Magnesium contributes to muscle and nerve function.

items.title: Low glycemic index
items.content: Helps stabilize blood sugar levels, beneficial for people with diabetes.

items.title: Antioxidant properties
items.content: Phenolic compounds protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Sorghum allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to sorghum or its products.

items.title: Phytic acid content
items.content: Phytic acid can reduce the absorption of certain minerals; soaking or fermenting can mitigate this.

items.title: Added ingredients
items.content: When purchasing, check for added ingredients that may contain gluten.

content.title: How to Use
content.content: Sorghum flour can be used in gluten‑free baking (bread, muffins, cookies), as a coating for frying, as a thickener in sauces and soups, and added to smoothies for extra nutrition.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store sorghum flour in an airtight container in a cool, dry place. For longer shelf life, keep it in the refrigerator or freezer to prevent fat oxidation.
